front: What COPY option previews all staged-file errors, including earlier partial loads?
why: Unlike RETURN_ERRORS, RETURN_ALL_ERRORS includes errors in previously partially loaded files. It validates without inserting rows.
trap: RETURN_ERRORS is not identical to RETURN_ALL_ERRORS.
code: COPY INTO orders FROM @s VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS;

front: Which COPY option skips bad rows but loads valid rows from the same file?
why: This loads valid records and reports errors for individual invalid rows; a source file may become PARTIALLY_LOADED.
trap: Different from SKIP_FILE, which skips the entire affected file.
code: COPY INTO orders FROM @s ON_ERROR = CONTINUE;

front: Which COPY option rejects a file if any record fails?
why: The entire error-containing file is skipped; other valid files may still be ingested.
trap: ABORT_STATEMENT aborts the whole load, not just the bad file.
code: COPY INTO orders FROM @s ON_ERROR = SKIP_FILE;

front: What is the default ON_ERROR for bulk COPY INTO?
why: A load error causes the COPY command to abort rather than silently skip invalid rows.
trap: Do not assume CONTINUE is the default.

front: Which COPY option deliberately reloads already-loaded files?
why: Bulk COPY normally remembers load history and skips known files; FORCE overrides this protection and can duplicate rows.
trap: FORCE does not deduplicate target rows.
code: COPY INTO t FROM @s FORCE = TRUE;

front: Which COPY option removes successfully loaded staged files?
why: PURGE requests that loaded files be deleted from the stage when the load succeeds. Cloud permissions still matter.
trap: PURGE is not a DELETE FROM target table.
code: COPY INTO t FROM @s PURGE = TRUE;

front: What does VALIDATION_MODE do to target-table row counts?
why: VALIDATION_MODE inspects staged files for errors but performs no data load.
trap: Unsupported when the COPY statement transforms data during loading.
code: COPY INTO t FROM @s VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ERRORS;

front: Can COPY INTO load transformations use LATERAL FLATTEN?
why: Snowflake does not support FLATTEN as part of the COPY INTO transformation subset. Load VARIANT first, then FLATTEN with SQL.
trap: FLATTEN itself is valid in normal SELECT queries.
code: SELECT f.value FROM raw, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => raw.payload:items) f;

front: What SQL command loads staged files into a Snowflake table?
why: The destination is a table and the source is a stage.
trap: Reverse the direction to unload query results.

front: What SQL command unloads data into files in a stage?
why: For unloading, the destination after INTO is a stage or cloud location.
trap: PUT uploads local files; it does not export query results.
code: COPY INTO @archive FROM (SELECT * FROM sales) FILE_FORMAT=(TYPE=CSV);

front: What does COPY INTO <location> PARTITION BY do?
back: Partitions exported rows into different output paths/files
why: PARTITION BY in unloading influences the generated output files, not the native table layout.
trap: Not the same as CLUSTER BY on a Snowflake table.
code: COPY INTO @out FROM (SELECT * FROM t) PARTITION BY (region);

front: Large nightly files, existing warehouse, no near-real-time SLA: choose what?
why: Bulk COPY fits controlled, large batches. Cost depends on real workload and warehouse use; serverless is not always cheapest.
trap: Do not choose Snowpipe solely because it sounds cheaper.

front: Files arriving frequently with minute-level freshness: choose what?
why: Snowpipe uses Snowflake-managed compute and cloud notifications to load newly arriving staged files.
trap: It does not use the BI warehouse, unlike bulk COPY.

front: Direct Kafka row events, seconds latency, no staged files: choose what?
why: Snowpipe Streaming ingests streaming rows with low latency through supported APIs/connectors.
trap: Classic Snowpipe consumes files, not individual Kafka rows.

front: Who provides compute for classic Snowpipe?
why: You do not assign a customer-managed warehouse to a pipe; Snowflake manages ingest compute.
trap: Separate from ordinary COPY INTO using a warehouse.

front: How is classic Snowpipe ingestion billed today?
why: Snowpipe billing changed from the older per-file model; evaluate current credits and compute cost by actual load volume.
trap: Avoid outdated per-file billing claims.

front: Snowpipe stopped loading one S3 prefix. What is the first check?
back: Cloud event notifications and path/prefix filters
why: Auto-ingest only receives the paths matched by the bucket’s notification configuration and pipe location.
trap: A suspended BI warehouse is not a reason for serverless Snowpipe to stop.

front: Which SQL statement checks ingestion pipe status?
why: The system function gives information about the operational status of a Snowpipe pipe.
trap: Do not confuse with SYSTEM$EXTERNAL_TABLE_PIPE_STATUS.

front: How do external tables store their row data?
back: In external cloud storage, not imported native storage
why: External tables store metadata that references files, providing read-only SQL access to their contents.
trap: Do not confuse external tables with writable Iceberg tables.

front: How are external table file listings updated?
back: Metadata refresh, manual or cloud-event driven
why: ALTER EXTERNAL TABLE ... REFRESH updates file metadata; supported cloud notifications can enable auto refresh.
trap: New files are not automatically visible without metadata being updated.

front: Which external table pseudocolumn contains the source file path?
why: This identifies the file source associated with a row in supported stage/external-table contexts.
trap: METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER is the row position, not the filename.

front: Which external-table pseudocolumn holds the row value?
why: External tables expose a VALUE variant field containing a row representation from external files.
trap: METADATA$FILENAME is not the record body.

front: Which Snowflake function is used for external table auto-refresh pipe status?
why: This function provides information about the pipe that supports automatic metadata refresh for an external table.
trap: It is distinct from SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS for a named Snowpipe.

front: Can UPDATE/DELETE modify an ordinary external table’s cloud files?
back: No; ordinary external tables are read-only
why: External-table metadata points to files that Snowflake queries rather than owns for regular DML.
trap: Iceberg tables have different DML capabilities.

front: What JSON format option splits a top-level JSON array into rows?
why: If a file is one outer array containing objects, the loader can treat array elements as separate records.
trap: Different from STRIP_NULL_VALUES.
code: CREATE FILE FORMAT jf TYPE=JSON STRIP_OUTER_ARRAY=TRUE;

front: Which CSV setting skips the first line of a file?
why: SKIP_HEADER is a CSV file format setting to skip lines at the start of each file.
trap: It does not parse JSON arrays.

front: Which CSV setting allows commas inside quoted fields?
why: Set this to a supported quote character, e.g. double quotes, so delimiters within quoted text are parsed as field content.
trap: Does not control compression or skipping headers.

front: How do you reuse parsing options across many COPY jobs?
why: CREATE FILE FORMAT stores delimiter, encoding, quote and compression settings as a reusable object.
trap: Different from STORAGE INTEGRATION, which authorizes cloud access.
code: CREATE FILE FORMAT my_csv TYPE=CSV SKIP_HEADER=1;

front: Which internal stage reference means “my user stage”?
why: Every Snowflake user has a user stage. A stage is not a table; files must still be loaded for native storage.
trap: @%orders refers to an orders table stage.

front: Which internal stage reference means a specific table’s stage?
why: Snowflake provisions a table stage associated with each table, referenced with @%.
trap: A named stage is @stage_name.

front: Which command uploads a local file to an internal stage?
why: PUT sends a file from a local client to a Snowflake internal stage in supported clients.
trap: GET downloads files; both have client restrictions.

front: Which command downloads an internal-stage file to a local machine?
why: GET downloads staged files to a local filesystem from supported clients.
trap: COPY INTO @stage unloads table/query data to stage; GET downloads the files.

front: External S3 stage references integration S3_INT with which property?
why: External stages can use integration objects to avoid embedded long-lived credentials.
trap: INTEGRATION= is not the correct stage clause.

front: Why is an AWS external ID needed in an IAM trust relationship?
why: A trust policy uses the Snowflake IAM principal and external ID to ensure role assumption comes from the intended party.
trap: It does not itself encrypt data in transit.

front: Why split a single giant compressed load file into many files?
back: Improve parallel loading across compute nodes
why: Multiple files can be processed concurrently; one enormous unsplittable file limits parallelism.
trap: Official sizing guidance is roughly 100–250 MB or larger compressed, workload-dependent.

front: Which table function inspects a previous COPY job’s load errors?
why: VALIDATE examines errors associated with a previous load job, unlike staged-file VALIDATION_MODE.
trap: It is not a way to validate newly arrived files without a job.

front: Where can you inspect recent COPY load statuses?
why: COPY_HISTORY exposes information about file loads and statuses such as PARTIALLY_LOADED.
trap: QUERY_HISTORY and COPY_HISTORY answer different questions.

front: Which function expands a VARIANT array into relational rows?
why: The table function emits one row per nested array element while preserving access to parent row columns.
trap: Allowed in SELECT; not inside COPY transformation.
code: SELECT t.id, f.value FROM t, LATERAL FLATTEN(input=>t.payload:items) f;

front: Which function converts JSON-formatted VARCHAR text into VARIANT?
why: PARSE_JSON parses the string into semi-structured Snowflake data for path extraction.
trap: TO_JSON does the reverse: VARIANT to JSON text.

front: Which function changes VARIANT JSON null into SQL NULL?
why: Snowflake distinguishes JSON null inside VARIANT from SQL NULL; STRIP_NULL_VALUE converts the former.
trap: IS_NULL_VALUE tests JSON null rather than transforming it.

front: Which Snowflake layer compiles and optimizes SQL?
why: Cloud Services manages SQL parsing, optimization, metadata, access control and coordination.
trap: Virtual warehouses execute data processing.

front: Which Snowflake layer holds immutable micro-partitions?
why: Durable Snowflake table data is stored in encrypted, compressed columnar micro-partitions, separate from warehouses.
trap: Warehouse SSDs are cache, not the durable storage layer.

front: Which layer actually executes joins and aggregations?
why: Warehouse compute reads data and executes operations, while Cloud Services compiles and coordinates.
trap: Metadata services are not the heavy query execution engine.

front: Best way to isolate heavy ETL from BI query contention?
why: Independent warehouses share underlying Snowflake data but isolate compute resources.
trap: Separate databases alone do not guarantee compute isolation.

front: What is the principal purpose of multi-cluster warehouses?
back: Handle concurrent queries and reduce queuing
why: Additional clusters handle separate workloads/queries concurrently, not necessarily one slow query.
trap: Scale up a warehouse for single-query memory pressure.

front: What happens to warehouse local data cache on suspend?
why: The warehouse compute instances and their SSD cache disappear on suspension.
trap: The persisted result cache is independent of warehouse suspension.

front: Can eligible cached query results be returned while the warehouse is suspended?
why: Persisted query results can be served without running warehouse compute when reuse criteria are met.
trap: A changing underlying table can invalidate eligibility.

front: How long can an eligible persisted result be reused initially?
why: Snowflake persists query results for 24 hours initially and reuse can extend availability under stated limits.
trap: Do not confuse with warehouse local cache lifetime.

front: Can Snowflake micro-partitions be updated in place?
why: UPDATE and DELETE create replacement micro-partitions while old versions remain subject to retention rules.
trap: No manual VACUUM required for ordinary native tables.

front: How does Snowflake skip unrelated storage blocks in a filtered query?
why: The optimizer uses micro-partition metadata such as min/max value ranges to skip irrelevant partitions.
trap: Clustering can improve pruning but is not always necessary.

front: Which feature lets you UNDROP a recently dropped table yourself?
why: Time Travel enables querying/restoring prior table states within configured retention; UNDROP is self-service SQL.
trap: Fail-safe is Snowflake-managed recovery, not a user UNDROP command.

front: Can a customer issue SQL to recover directly from Fail-safe?
why: Fail-safe is a Snowflake-managed emergency recovery period, not an ordinary queryable historical period.
trap: Time Travel is for normal customer-directed restoration.

front: Need cross-session persistence without Fail-safe: which table type?
why: Transient tables persist until dropped but omit Fail-safe and have limited Time Travel options.
trap: Temporary tables are session-scoped.

front: Which table type disappears when its creating session ends?
why: Temporary tables are scoped to a session and are removed when that session ends.
trap: TRANSIENT persists beyond the session.

front: Why is CREATE TABLE ... CLONE fast and storage-efficient initially?
why: Zero-copy clones initially reference existing storage; new storage appears as source/clone diverge.
trap: A clone is writable, not just a view.

front: Which Snowflake table type offers open-format interoperability and DML?
why: Snowflake Iceberg tables use open table format metadata while supporting writes in supported configurations.
trap: An ordinary external table is read-only.

front: What object connects an Iceberg table to external cloud storage?
why: An external volume defines access and storage locations for Iceberg data/metadata files in customer-managed cloud storage.
trap: Storage integrations typically support external stages.

front: What is the role of a catalog integration for Iceberg?
back: Connect Snowflake to an external Iceberg catalog
why: Catalog integrations coordinate table metadata/catalog operations; storage location is a separate concern.
trap: Do not confuse catalog integration with external volume.

front: Which object maintains a SELECT transformation based on TARGET_LAG?
why: Dynamic tables declaratively maintain transformations and schedule refreshes using target lag.
trap: Standard views do not materialize data by target lag.
code: CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE dt TARGET_LAG='15 minutes' WAREHOUSE=wh AS SELECT ...;

front: When does a stream offset advance after DML consumption?
why: A failed/rolled-back transaction does not consume the stream offset.
trap: SELECT alone does not advance a stream.

front: What coordinates scheduled, ordered SQL transformations?
why: Tasks run SQL or stored procedures on schedules/triggers and can form dependency graphs.
trap: Pipes handle staged-file ingestion, not arbitrary SQL orchestration.

front: Which scheduled task type needs no user-selected warehouse?
why: A serverless task uses Snowflake-managed compute instead of a WAREHOUSE clause.
trap: Snowpipe is not a general-purpose SQL task scheduler.

front: Natural language question over sales tables → SQL: which feature?
why: Cortex Analyst supports NL-to-SQL over structured data using semantic definitions.
trap: Cortex Search retrieves text for RAG.

front: Semantic retrieval over support PDFs for RAG: which feature?
why: Cortex Search builds managed retrieval over text content, helping ground generated answers.
trap: Cortex Analyst is for natural language over structured SQL datasets.

front: Which Snowflake component manages trained model versions and inference methods?
why: Snowflake Model Registry stores and manages model versions and registered methods for inference.
trap: Different from pretrained Cortex AI functions.

front: Where do supported Snowpark DataFrame transformations run?
why: Snowpark builds plans that execute within Snowflake rather than exporting all table rows to the client.
trap: DataFrame construction can be lazy until an action.

front: Which programmable object can be called as a scalar SELECT expression?
why: UDFs return a value for SQL expressions; procedures support multi-statement operations invoked with CALL.
trap: Do not use stored procedures as drop-in scalar expressions.

front: What does DIRECTORY=(ENABLE=TRUE) on a stage enable?
why: Directory tables expose staged file path/metadata information for SQL discovery.
trap: Enabling alone does not ensure auto-refresh notifications.

front: Which function builds a scoped file URL to a staged file?
why: Scoped URLs provide controlled time/query-context-based access to staged files.
trap: BUILD_STAGE_FILE_URL produces a different, stage-based file URL.

front: Minimum edition for Tri-Secret Secure?
why: Tri-Secret Secure combines Snowflake- and customer-managed keys and is a Business Critical feature.
trap: Periodic rekeying has a different edition requirement.

front: Minimum edition for periodic rekeying?
why: Periodic rekeying is an Enterprise-and-higher feature per Snowflake’s edition matrix.
trap: Some third-party mocks incorrectly say Business Critical.

front: GRANT ROLE ANALYST TO ROLE MANAGER: who inherits whom?
why: Privileges flow from a child/granted role upward to the receiving parent role.
trap: Reversing the direction is a common exam trap.
code: GRANT ROLE ANALYST TO ROLE MANAGER;

front: Table SELECT exists, database USAGE exists, but access denied: likely missing?
why: Snowflake object access normally requires privileges on the table and enclosing database and schema.
trap: Table SELECT alone does not guarantee schema access.
code: GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA db.s TO ROLE reporter;

front: Which privilege lets a role run SQL on a warehouse?
why: USAGE permits the role to use warehouse compute. MODIFY or OPERATE is for warehouse management.
trap: USAGE on database/schema/table is separately necessary.
code: GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE wh TO ROLE analyst;

front: What global privilege allows broad administration of grants?
why: MANAGE GRANTS lets a role manage grants without owning each object.
trap: MONITOR USAGE is not grant administration.

front: Which role is intended for account data objects and warehouses?
why: SYSADMIN is the standard built-in role for managing databases, schemas, tables and warehouses.
trap: SECURITYADMIN focuses on grants/roles.

front: Which built-in role focuses on security grants and roles?
why: SECURITYADMIN manages access; USERADMIN is an inherited role for creating users and roles.
trap: Use ACCOUNTADMIN sparingly.

front: Who manages Snowflake accounts across an organization?
why: ORGADMIN is organization-level rather than per-account object management.
trap: ACCOUNTADMIN is specific to an individual account.

front: How can a role automatically SELECT tables created later in one schema?
why: Future grants apply designated privileges to new matching objects as they are created.
trap: Existing object grants do not automatically cover future tables.
code: GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA db.s TO ROLE r;

front: Who controls object grants in a managed access schema?
back: Schema owner or MANAGE GRANTS role
why: Managed access centralizes grants and restricts ordinary object owners from independently granting privileges.
trap: Different from a regular schema’s ownership privileges.

front: Which policy changes sensitive column values by role?
why: Dynamic Data Masking applies a policy to a column, returning redacted or original values based on conditions.
trap: Row access policies filter rows, not individual field values.

front: Which policy filters which table rows are visible?
why: Row access policies apply a predicate controlling row visibility at query time.
trap: Column masking is a separate mechanism.

front: What function checks whether an account role is active in the session hierarchy?
why: Role membership can include inherited/secondary roles; this is more complete than CURRENT_ROLE for many policy checks.
trap: CURRENT_ROLE returns primary active role, not all hierarchy membership.

front: Tag created + masking policy created, but still unmasked: what was omitted?
back: Associate the masking policy with the tag
why: Tag-based masking requires an explicit policy association; tags alone provide metadata/classification.
trap: A tag is not automatically an enforcement mechanism.

front: Which policy restricts access from disallowed IP ranges?
why: Network policies block connection origins using allowed/blocked IP or network rules.
trap: Authentication policies govern login methods, not source IP ranges.

front: Which policy controls permitted methods such as password versus SSO?
why: Authentication policies govern allowed authentication methods and related controls.
trap: Different from Network Policies that regulate network origin.

front: What is federated authentication for Snowflake?
why: SSO can delegate proving identity to an IdP while Snowflake RBAC still grants object permissions.
trap: Authentication and authorization are not the same.

front: Which Account Usage view tracks accessed objects and columns?
why: ACCESS_HISTORY exposes accessed objects and columns useful for governance and lineage investigations.
trap: QUERY_HISTORY is centered on query executions and metrics.

front: Which Account Usage view shows SQL runtime, status, and history?
why: ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY is account-wide historical execution metadata; it may have reporting latency.
trap: Not a substitute for column-level access auditing.

front: Which schema offers database-scoped, mostly current object metadata?
why: INFORMATION_SCHEMA is database scoped and subject to visibility/privileges.
trap: ACCOUNT_USAGE provides broader historical account reports with latency.

front: What can object tags accomplish besides data classification?
why: Tags can label objects by cost center, application or sensitivity, supporting governance and usage analysis.
trap: Tags alone do not mask data without policy linkage.

front: Can a permanent Enterprise table configure more than one day of Time Travel?
why: Enterprise+ supports configurable retention up to 90 days on eligible permanent tables.
trap: Transient/temporary table retention rules differ.

front: What is the difference between CURRENT_ROLE and IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION?
back: Primary role vs membership in active role hierarchy
why: CURRENT_ROLE names the primary role; IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION tests whether the named account role is active in the session.
trap: Masks based only on CURRENT_ROLE can miss inherited role contexts.

front: Can a consumer SELECT through a secure view without seeing its definition?
why: Secure views obscure sensitive query logic from non-owners, while exposing authorized rows/columns.
trap: Standard views do not provide identical definition-hiding semantics.

front: Which feature can suspend warehouses at credit thresholds?
why: Resource monitors support threshold alerts and suspension actions for user-managed warehouse credit usage.
trap: They do not cap every class of serverless billing.

front: Unquoted Snowflake identifiers normally resolve in which case?
why: Unquoted names normalize to uppercase; double-quoted identifiers preserve exact case by default.
trap: Quoted mixed case must be referenced with exact case.

front: Does Snowflake encrypt data at rest automatically?
why: Snowflake provides encryption at rest by default; customer-controlled key features are optional and edition-dependent.
trap: Tri-Secret Secure is not required for baseline encryption.

front: What must be enabled to let a role use a table and run a query?
back: Warehouse USAGE + DB/schema USAGE + object SELECT
why: RBAC has separate gates for compute and reading the data object.
trap: Granting ACCOUNTADMIN for convenience is not least privilege.

front: For regional row filtering AND email redaction, choose which policies?
why: Use row access for geographic restriction and masking for sensitive column values.
trap: One policy does not automatically replace the other.

front: Single long join spilling to remote disk: scale up or out?
why: Remote spill suggests memory pressure for an individual query; a larger warehouse can provide resources per query.
trap: Multiple clusters target concurrency, not one heavy query.

front: Hundreds of small queries queue at 9 a.m.: scale up or out?
why: Additional clusters can handle concurrent queries, reducing queue time.
trap: Single-query compute may already be sufficient.

front: Cost prioritized over queue latency: STANDARD or ECONOMY policy?
why: ECONOMY multi-cluster scaling is more conservative about adding clusters to reduce credit usage.
trap: STANDARD adds clusters sooner to minimize queuing.

front: Latency prioritized over cost in a multi-cluster warehouse: which policy?
why: STANDARD favors reducing queueing delay by scaling clusters more readily.
trap: ECONOMY may tolerate more queue time.

front: Huge table, equality filter on scattered IDs: which optimization?
why: SOS builds access paths for selective point lookups, trading maintenance for latency improvement.
trap: Clustering is often better for recurring range/pruning patterns.

front: Huge table, repeated date-range filters and poor pruning: which option?
why: Clustering reduces micro-partition overlap for common predicates, improving pruning on suitable large tables.
trap: Clustering costs maintenance credits; not every table needs it.

front: Repeated supported expensive aggregate on slowly changing table: which feature?
why: A materialized view maintains precomputed results to speed repeated compatible queries.
trap: Dynamic tables support broader joins/transformations with target lag.

front: What should you fix first if Query Profile shows CartesianJoin explosion?
why: Missing/incorrect join predicates can multiply rows; more compute cannot correct unintended cartesian semantics.
trap: Beware accidental many-to-many joins too.

front: Which SYSTEM$ function estimates Query Acceleration benefits?
why: This function can assess eligible candidate queries for Query Acceleration Service.
trap: QAS is not guaranteed to accelerate every query.

front: Which Account Usage view identifies Query Acceleration candidates?
why: It provides query-level eligibility metrics useful for deciding whether QAS may help.
trap: Do not assume every GROUP BY is eligible.

front: What does BYTES_SPILLED_TO_REMOTE_STORAGE imply?
back: Intermediate query data exceeded available memory/local resources
why: The engine spilled intermediate working sets to remote storage, typically slowing execution.
trap: Different from ordinary scanning of remote table storage.

front: High partitions scanned despite selective filter: what might help?
back: Improve pruning via clustering or search optimization
why: Choose based on predicates, data size and maintenance costs; range/pruning vs equality lookup have different best options.
trap: Do not always resize the warehouse first.

front: What setting can disable persisted query-result reuse?
why: This setting can be used to separate persisted result-cache hits from actual query execution.
trap: Warehouse local cache may still speed data scanning.

front: What turns a semi-structured array into multiple rows in SELECT?
why: LATERAL FLATTEN preserves parent context while emitting rows for each array element.
trap: ARRAY_AGG combines rows into an array, the reverse direction.
code: SELECT f.value FROM t, LATERAL FLATTEN(input => t.v:items) f;

front: What does QUALIFY filter?
why: QUALIFY is evaluated after window functions, analogous to HAVING for aggregates.
trap: WHERE cannot directly reference window function output.
code: SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts DESC) rn FROM t QUALIFY rn=1;

front: Which SQL constructs support hierarchical or recursive queries?
why: Snowflake supports recursive CTEs and hierarchical CONNECT BY queries.
trap: QUALIFY filters windows rather than traversing hierarchies.

front: Which function returns VARIANT as JSON-formatted VARCHAR?
why: TO_JSON serializes a VARIANT; PARSE_JSON parses string text into VARIANT.
trap: Do not confuse OBJECT_CONSTRUCT with TO_JSON.

front: What do type predicates (e.g., IS_ARRAY) do?
back: Test the type of a VARIANT value
why: They return Boolean type checks; type casts like TO_VARCHAR change representation.
trap: Do not mistake type predicates for conversion functions.

front: Case-insensitive SQL wildcard matching uses what?
why: ILIKE supports SQL % and _ pattern syntax without case sensitivity.
trap: LIKE is usually case-sensitive; REGEXP_LIKE uses regex syntax.

front: SUBSTR(text, -2, 2) reads from which position?
why: Negative starts count backward from the end. Zero starts count as one.
trap: A negative length returns an empty string.

front: Does CONCAT_WS skip NULL arguments in Snowflake?
back: No; any NULL argument gives NULL
why: Snowflake CONCAT_WS does not skip NULL the way some other database engines do.
trap: Use COALESCE for explicit replacements.

front: Which function gets one delimited token as a scalar?
why: SPLIT_PART uses one-based part indexing. SPLIT returns an array; SPLIT_TO_TABLE returns rows.
trap: The third argument is a field index, not character position.

front: Which function splits a VARCHAR into multiple SQL rows?
why: SPLIT_TO_TABLE emits rows with SEQ, INDEX and VALUE.
trap: SPLIT returns an ARRAY, not separate rows.

front: Which function counts characters, not UTF-8 bytes?
why: LENGTH measures character count; OCTET_LENGTH measures bytes. Unicode characters can occupy multiple bytes.
trap: BIT_LENGTH returns bits, not characters.

front: Which function removes leading AND trailing spaces?
why: TRIM removes specified characters (spaces by default) from both ends; LTRIM/RTRIM target a single side.
trap: TRIM does not remove all interior whitespace.

front: Which function capitalizes word beginnings?
why: INITCAP changes text to initial-capital word format under Snowflake’s rules.
trap: LOWER and UPPER do not title-case words.

front: POSITION returns what kind of value?
why: POSITION/CHARINDEX finds the location of literal text; CONTAINS returns a Boolean.
trap: Do not mix a number-returning search with CONTAINS.

front: REPLACE versus TRANSLATE: what is the distinction?
why: REPLACE targets literal substrings, TRANSLATE maps individual characters one-to-one.
trap: REGEXP_REPLACE uses patterns rather than literal text.

front: What regex function tests whether a VARCHAR matches a pattern?
why: Snowflake REGEXP_LIKE uses regular expressions and implicitly anchors the pattern at both ends.
trap: Use .* for an embedded substring.

front: How does Snowflake REGEXP_LIKE handle an unanchored pattern?
back: As implicitly anchored at both ends
why: A pattern like 123 does not match the entire string abc123; add .* around the substring.
trap: Regex is not SQL LIKE and does not use % as wildcard.

front: What does REGEXP_REPLACE default occurrence=0 mean?
why: Default occurrence=0 replaces every match; positive occurrences can target one.
trap: Default replacement is an empty string.

front: Which function extracts a matched substring using regex?
why: REGEXP_SUBSTR returns matched text; REGEXP_INSTR returns match position; REGEXP_COUNT counts matches.
trap: REGEXP_LIKE returns BOOLEAN.

front: Which function reverses character order?
why: REVERSE is a string function that returns input characters in reverse order.
trap: REVERSING is not the correct function name.

front: Which function pads a string on the LEFT?
why: LPAD fills or truncates a string to the requested total length, using a pad pattern.
trap: RPAD pads the right side.

front: Which function repeats a string n times?
why: REPEAT returns a specified input text multiple times; SPACE creates spaces.
trap: Do not confuse with LPAD/RPAD.

front: Which function returns how many regex matches occur?
why: REGEXP_COUNT counts matching pattern occurrences in text.
trap: REGEXP_INSTR returns the position of a match.

front: What is the difference between STARTSWITH and CONTAINS?
